title: Language Attrition & Maintenance

pts: Language attrition describes the genuine erosion of proficiency in a previously acquired language, whether L1 or L2, due to reduced use.
This is distinct from simply forgetting isolated vocabulary — attrition can affect grammar, fluency, and phonology systematically.
This phenomenon affects both L1 attrition (in emigrant or heritage-language communities) and L2 attrition (in learners who stop using a studied language).

v: Teacher education; trainee teachers, or B2 learners

items: Participants list every language they have known, even a little.
For each, they mark current ability in listening, speaking, reading and writing (strong, some, lost).
They note when and why any ability declined.
In pairs, they compare which skills declined and which survived.
Plenary: what patterns appear across the group?
With school learners, focus on one language, for example a language spoken by grandparents.
Support: provide a table with the four skills already drawn.
Challenge: participants distinguish never-acquired skills from skills that were lost.

blocks.x: From a trainee’s language history (written for this book):

lines: Tulu: grew up with it at my grandmother’s house. I still understand it but speak it slowly now.
Hindi: studied at school. I can read signs and follow films, but I would struggle to write a letter.

blocks.x: Attrition is not the same as never having learned: the trainee once spoke Tulu fluently.

body: Purpose: to show uneven loss across languages and skills. Content: a table of three languages against four skills, each cell shaded strong, some or lost, with a small timeline beneath. Style: clear grid, labels as well as shading. Board version: a hand-drawn grid with ticks and dashes.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a group summary of language histories.

blocks.x: A language-history template drawn in the notebook.

pts: Emigrants and long-term expatriates sometimes experience measurable attrition in their own first language, particularly after extended reduced use.
This connects to Unit 88's subtractive-bilingualism concept — a language can decline even when it was originally the stronger, native one.
This is a genuinely under-discussed dimension of bilingual and multilingual life, worth including for completeness.

items: Prepare interview questions together in class (see model language).
Learners interview a relative or neighbour who lived for many years away from their home-language community.
Learners note the answers in English and report back in groups.
Groups identify what the person found harder in the home language after years away.
Learners conduct the interview in the home language and summarize in English, a mediation task (Unit 64).
Support: provide five fixed questions.
Challenge: learners add follow-up questions and write a short report.

lines: How long did you live away? Which language did you use most there?
When you came back, what was difficult in your home language?
Did you forget words, mix languages, or feel slower?
My uncle worked in Dubai for twenty years. He says his Kannada is fine at home, but he finds formal Kannada in letters difficult now.

blocks.x: First-language attrition is under-discussed, but common among long-term migrants (Schmid 2011).

body: Purpose: to show L1 attrition as a lived experience. Content: an older man with a suitcase returning to a family home, with speech bubbles in which a few words are faded. Style: warm, respectful. Board version: a house and a figure with a faded speech bubble.

items: Vocaroo (free) for recording short interview extracts, with consent.

blocks.x: Interview notes written in the notebook.

body: Adults adopted from Korea into French-speaking families as children showed little measurable knowledge of Korean in the study by Pallier and colleagues (2003). When use stops early and completely, even a first language can be almost entirely lost.

pts: L2 skills built through classroom study, without ongoing use, tend to decline measurably over subsequent months and years.
This directly reinforces Unit 56's advanced-autonomy argument for sustained, self-directed practice beyond any formal course's end.
This connects to Unit 47's plateau discussion — maintaining, not just achieving, proficiency requires its own deliberate strategy.

v: 20 minutes before and after a long holiday

items: Before the summer vacation, give a short quiz covering vocabulary, a listening item and a short writing task.
Keep the results; do not grade them.
Give an equivalent quiz in the first week after the vacation.
Compare scores by section.
Share the pattern with learners and ask who read or listened to English over the holiday.
Compare learners who took part in a holiday reading programme with those who did not, cautiously (Unit 81).
Support: shorter quiz for weaker learners.
Challenge: learners analyse their own before-and-after results.

lines: Vocabulary: 14.2 before, 11.8 after. Listening: 7.1 before, 6.9 after. Writing: 6.0 before, 4.5 after.
T: Which section dropped most?
S1: Writing. We did not write anything in the holidays.

blocks.x: Productive skills tend to decline faster than receptive ones; Bahrick (1984) found that most loss happens early and then stabilizes.

body: Purpose: to show uneven decline across skills. Content: three pairs of bars (vocabulary, listening, writing), with the writing pair showing the largest drop. Style: clean bar chart, marked ‘illustrative’. Board version: three pairs of chalk bars.

items: Google Forms (free) quiz mode for quick scoring.

blocks.x: Paper quizzes marked with a simple answer key.

pts: Productive skills (speaking, writing) tend to attrite faster and more visibly than receptive skills (listening, reading comprehension).
Vocabulary, particularly less frequent items, tends to erode before core grammatical structures do.
Understanding this pattern helps target maintenance strategy at the specific skills most vulnerable to decline.

items: Give learners a grid of can-do statements for receptive and productive skills.
Learners imagine one year with no English at all and mark which abilities they think they would lose first.
Show the research pattern: productive skills and less frequent vocabulary tend to decline first; core grammar and receptive skills last longer (Schmid 2011).
Learners choose the two most vulnerable abilities for themselves.
They plan one small activity to protect each.
Use the grid again at the end of the year as a self-assessment tool (Unit 42).
Support: fewer statements, in simple English with home-language support.
Challenge: learners explain why frequent words might survive longer.

lines: I can understand a short news report. (receptive)
I can write a clear email to a teacher. (productive)
I can use words like ‘reluctant’ and ‘obvious’ correctly. (less frequent vocabulary)
Writing: one short diary entry in English every Sunday. Vocabulary: one English article each week, noting three words.

body: Purpose: to show the typical order of loss. Content: a tree whose outer leaves (rare words, speaking, writing) are falling while the trunk and main branches (core grammar, listening, reading) remain. Style: gentle, clear labels. Board version: a trunk and branches with a few leaves falling.

items: Quizlet (free basic version) for learners’ own vocabulary sets.

blocks.x: A can-do grid glued into the notebook.

pts: Regular, even modest, ongoing use — extending Unit 31 and 32's extensive input principles beyond course completion — substantially slows attrition.
This connects directly to Unit 48's autonomous-learning skill, now applied to maintenance rather than initial acquisition.
Even brief, regular engagement outperforms occasional, intensive but infrequent re-engagement for maintenance purposes.

items: Ask learners which is better: two hours once a month, or ten minutes a day.
Explain that spaced, regular practice supports retention better than occasional intensive practice (Cepeda et al. 2006).
Learners choose small activities they can sustain: reading, listening, speaking, writing.
They fill in a weekly plan with one activity per day, each under fifteen minutes.
Check plans in pairs for realism.
Learners form WhatsApp groups that share one English item a day.
Support: provide a menu of ready activities.
Challenge: learners set measurable targets and review them monthly.

blocks.x: A learner’s weekly plan (written for this book):

lines: Monday: one graded reader chapter (Unit 31). Tuesday: English news on the radio. Wednesday: voice message to a friend in English. Thursday: diary entry. Friday: one podcast episode (Unit 32). Saturday: a film with English subtitles. Sunday: review new words.

blocks.x: The habit continues the autonomous learning skills of Unit 48, now aimed at keeping, not only gaining, a language.

body: Purpose: to contrast spaced and intensive practice. Content: two calendars; one with a small mark on every day and a steady line of retention above, the other with one large block per month and a zig-zag line that falls between blocks. Style: clear. Board version: two rows of boxes.

items: Anki (free on desktop and Android; paid on iOS) for spaced review; BBC Learning English (free) for short listening.

blocks.x: A paper habit tracker with seven boxes for each week.

body: Help learners choose maintenance activities they enjoy. A daily cricket commentary in English or a favourite song lyric will survive longer than a grammar workbook that feels like homework.

pts: Heritage speakers — those who grew up with a home language different from their community's dominant language — face particular attrition risks worth understanding.
This connects to Unit 88's bilingualism content, addressing heritage-language programmes as a specific institutional response.
Heritage-language teaching often demands genuinely different pedagogy than foreign-language teaching for the same target language.

blocks.x: A heritage learner is not a beginner

v: Teacher education; teachers of Indian languages or English

items: Present two learners in the same Kannada class: a heritage learner and a foreign-language learner (see model language).
Groups list what each can already do and what each needs.
Groups decide which activities would suit each learner.
Discuss why a single course for both might frustrate both (Montrul 2008; Polinsky 2018).
Apply the same comparison to a heritage learner of English, for example a child who returned from abroad.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Two learner profiles (written for this book):

lines: Rohan, 12, grew up in Pune. His parents speak Kannada at home. He understands family conversations, speaks informally, cannot read the script and makes grammar errors in formal speech.
Emma, 12, moved to Bengaluru last year from the UK. She is learning Kannada from the beginning, reads the script slowly and speaks little.

blocks.x: Rohan needs literacy, formal registers and confidence; Emma needs basic vocabulary and listening. Heritage learners often need different pedagogy from foreign-language learners of the same language.

body: Purpose: to show different profiles in the same class. Content: two bar profiles side by side, one high in listening and informal speaking but low in reading, the other low but even across skills. Style: clean. Board version: two sets of four bars.

items: StoryWeaver (free, Pratham Books) for levelled books in Kannada and other Indian languages.

blocks.x: Two profile cards drawn on paper.

pts: Course design should explicitly address post-course maintenance strategy, not just the acquisition happening within the course itself.
This connects to Unit 19's homework and Unit 56's autonomy content, extended explicitly to life after formal instruction ends.
This is a genuinely underrepresented consideration in most course design, worth deliberately including.

v: A course or Class 10 or 12 scheme of work

items: Look at the last month of a course or school year in your scheme of work (Unit 14).
Identify where learners are prepared for life after the course.
Design a two-lesson maintenance module: a self-check, a habit plan and a list of free resources.
Plan a follow-up message three months later.
For school leavers, link the module to homework and self-study skills (Unit 19) and learning contracts (Unit 56).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A maintenance module for Class 12 leavers (written for this book):

lines: Lesson 1: What will I lose? Self-check grid; the holiday data from our class.
Lesson 2: My plan. Habit plan; a list of free English resources; buddies for weekly messages.
Follow-up: a WhatsApp message in September asking each learner to report one English activity.

blocks.x: This is one of the most underrepresented stages in course design.

body: Purpose: to show maintenance as part of course design. Content: a course timeline drawn as a road, with a dotted continuation beyond the ‘end of course’ sign labelled ‘maintenance’. Style: simple. Board version: a solid line becoming a dotted line.

items: WhatsApp (free) broadcast lists for follow-up messages, with parental consent for minors.

blocks.x: A printed resource list and a postcard learners address to themselves, sent three months later.

pts: This series has focused heavily on acquisition; this poster reframes the full arc to include maintenance as an equally real, equally teachable phase.
Preparing learners for this full arc, not just initial achievement, reflects the same long-term, sustainable thinking Unit 72 applied to teachers themselves.
This closes a genuine gap in how language learning is typically framed and taught.

items: Teachers reflect: which aspects of their own English have become weaker since training?
They mark the grid for skills they use rarely, for example extended writing or informal conversation.
In pairs, they share one area and one realistic maintenance step.
They form a small group that meets or messages regularly to practise.
A DIET runs a monthly English reading circle for teachers in Kannada-medium schools.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s reflection (written for this book):

lines: I teach English in Classes 6 and 7 but speak it only in the lesson. My speaking is slower than at college. I will join the DIET reading circle and record a short weekly talk.

blocks.x: The learning arc has two phases, acquisition and maintenance, and both apply to teachers too (Unit 72).

body: Purpose: to reframe learning as acquisition plus maintenance. Content: an arc rising from ‘beginning’ to ‘proficient’, then continuing level along a path marked ‘maintenance’, with a teacher and a learner walking together. Style: warm. Board version: a curve followed by a flat line.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India platform) for teacher professional resources.

blocks.x: A teachers’ reading circle using library books and newspapers.

body: In your last lesson before a long holiday, ask each learner to write one English activity they will do every week and seal it in an envelope. Open the envelopes in the first lesson after the holiday and discuss honestly what happened.

dek: Unit 89 of 100: what happens to a language once it's no longer actively used or supported — a real, under-discussed phenomenon affecting learners and bilingual communities alike.

aims.x: Language teaching usually stops at acquisition. This unit looks at what happens afterwards: how languages, including English and learners’ home languages, can erode when they are no longer used, and what learners, teachers and schools can do to keep them. It treats maintenance as a phase of learning that can be planned and taught.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define language attrition and distinguish it from ordinary forgetting;
explain how first-language attrition occurs among migrants and in children;
describe the typical course of L2 attrition after formal study ends;
identify which skills and areas of language tend to decline first;
design a realistic, spaced maintenance plan with learners;
explain why heritage speakers need a different pedagogy from foreign-language learners;
include post-course maintenance in course and programme design.

why: Why this matters. Language teaching typically focuses on acquisition. Equally real is what happens afterward — languages, including English itself, can genuinely be lost or eroded.

background.x: Language attrition is the decline of proficiency in a language a person once knew, caused by reduced use rather than by illness or injury (Schmid 2011). It differs from forgetting a few words: attrition can affect fluency, grammar and pronunciation in systematic ways. It affects first languages, as among long-term migrants, and second languages, as among learners who stop using a language after leaving school or college.

Two classic studies mark the extremes. Harry Bahrick (1984) tested people who had learned Spanish at school, up to fifty years earlier. Much of what they lost disappeared in the first few years, but what remained after that stayed remarkably stable for decades, in what he called a ‘permastore’. At the other extreme, Christophe Pallier and colleagues (2003) studied adults adopted from Korea into French families in childhood, and found little measurable trace of Korean in their behaviour or brain responses. First languages can be lost almost entirely when use stops early; languages learned more fully and later tend to be more resilient.

Heritage speakers, who grow up with a home language that is not the main language of their wider community, form a special case. Silvina Montrul (2008) and Maria Polinsky (2018) show that heritage speakers’ grammars often differ from those of speakers raised in the homeland, partly because acquisition was incomplete and partly because of attrition. Heritage learners often understand far more than they can say, and need teaching that builds on this.

In India these questions are close to home. Children of families who move from Karnataka to Mumbai, Delhi or the Gulf may understand Kannada but struggle to speak or read it. Many learners in rural areas lose much of their school English after Class 10 or 12 when they have no reason to use it. NEP 2020 emphasizes the preservation of Indian languages (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 treats home languages as resources (NCERT 2023). Both goals require attention to maintenance, not only to initial learning. Unit 94 continues the theme at the level of whole communities.

items: Language biography. A written history of one’s languages showing which skills were lost or kept.
Holiday check report. Before-and-after data from one class, with a cautious interpretation.
Maintenance plan. A learner’s or teacher’s spaced weekly plan with measurable targets.
Module design. A two-lesson maintenance module added to a real scheme of work.
Which of your own languages has faded? What caused it?
What happens to your learners’ English after they leave your class?
How do you respond to heritage learners who understand much but speak little?
Does your course end with a plan for maintenance, or only with an exam?
What small, regular habit keeps your own English strong?
How could your school support children’s home languages as well as English?

reading: Bahrick, H. P. 1984. ‘Semantic memory content in permastore: fifty years of memory for Spanish learned in school’. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 113/1: 1–29.
Cepeda, N. J., H. Pashler, E. Vul, J. T. Wixted, and D. Rohrer. 2006. ‘Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis’. Psychological Bulletin 132/3: 354–80.
Ministry of Human Resource Development. 2020. National Education Policy 2020. New Delhi: Government of India.
Montrul, S. 2008. Incomplete Acquisition in Bilingualism: Re-examining the Age Factor. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
NCERT. 2023. National Curriculum Framework for School Education 2023. New Delhi: National Council of Educational Research and Training.

Pallier, C., S. Dehaene, J.-B. Poline, D. LeBihan, A.-M. Argenti, E. Dupoux, and J. Mehler. 2003. ‘Brain imaging of language plasticity in adopted adults: can a second language replace the first?’. Cerebral Cortex 13/2: 155–61.
Polinsky, M. 2018. Heritage Languages and Their Speakers. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Schmid, M. S. 2011. Language Attrition. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
perm: All language histories, profiles, interview questions, plans and data are original and written for this book; the before-and-after class results are fictional. Interviews with family members and recordings of learners require informed consent, and parental consent for minors. Screenshots of Google tools, Vocaroo, Quizlet, Anki, StoryWeaver, WhatsApp or DIKSHA require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: The gradual loss of proficiency in a first language, usually when a speaker has little opportunity to use it, for example after moving early to a place where another language dominates.

A person who grew up with a home language that is not the main language of their wider community, such as a Kannada-speaking child raised in Mumbai. Heritage speakers often understand more than they can say (Montrul 2008; Polinsky 2018).
The situation in which a heritage speaker’s home language is not fully developed because exposure decreased in childhood, often once schooling began in another language (Montrul 2008).
The decline in proficiency in a language a person once knew, caused by reduced use. It can affect both first and second languages.
Keeping a language alive and in use, whether a community keeping its language despite pressure to shift, or an individual keeping proficiency after formal study ends.
Bahrick’s (1984) term for knowledge that, after an initial period of forgetting, remains stable in memory for decades, such as some school foreign-language vocabulary.
Speaking and writing, the skills in which learners produce language, as opposed to the receptive skills of listening and reading.

The language skills of listening and reading, through which learners receive and understand language, as distinct from the productive skills of speaking and writing. Receptive ability is usually larger than, and often retained longer than, productive ability.

The loss of second-language ability after use or study stops, for example when school English is little used after leaving school. Productive skills and less frequent vocabulary are usually lost first; receptive knowledge tends to last longer.

Spreading study or practice over several sessions with gaps between them, rather than concentrating it in one block. Spaced practice leads to better long-term retention than cramming the night before an examination.
